opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so Tom's model — the compute-centric framework he built at Open Philanthropy — was a really important starting point, and a lot of what we did with GATE builds on it. But there were a few things we felt it didn't capture well, especially if you want to think about how actual economic actors make decisions about investing in AI.

The main one is that in Tom's model, investment in AI is largely set exogenously. You basically specify how fast spending on compute and training runs grows, and then you see what happens to capabilities and automation. But in reality, that investment is a choice. People put money into building bigger data centers and training bigger models because they expect a return on it. And the return depends on how much of the economy the AI can automate, how valuable that automation is, what the interest rate is, and so on. So we wanted a model where investment is endogenous — where you have something like a forward-looking agent that's deciding how to allocate resources between ordinary physical capital, compute hardware, and training, based on what that will actually yield.

That matters a lot for the dynamics. If you think that crossing some threshold of compute unlocks the automation of a large fraction of tasks, and those tasks represent a huge share of world GDP, then the rational response is to invest enormously right now, much more than people currently are. So the model gives you a kind of economic argument for why the investment ramp could be much steeper than a naive extrapolation would suggest.

The second thing is that we wanted to integrate the macroeconomic side more seriously. GATE has an explicit production function where AI and human labor substitute across tasks, there's capital accumulation, and there's a feedback loop from output back into investment. That lets you ask questions like what happens to wages, how fast output grows, and how sensitive all of this is to things like the elasticity of substitution or how much of the economy is bottlenecked by tasks that are hard to automate.

And the third piece was making it something people could play with. We built an interactive version so people could change the assumptions they disagree with and see how the conclusions shift, rather than just taking our headline numbers at face value. A lot of the disagreement in this space comes down to a few key parameters, and we wanted to make it easy to see which ones actually drive the results.

r001.rationale: The response says Davidson’s model specifies compute and training growth and then projects capabilities and automation, but it does not explain a mapping from effective compute increases to the share of economic tasks automated.

r002.rationale: It presents endogenous, forward-looking resource allocation based on expected returns as a central reason for GATE, which captures replacing fixed investment rules with value-based optimization.

r003.rationale: It does not say Davidson’s hardcoded rules could lead to unreasonable decisions under extreme parameter values.

r004.rationale: It describes investing heavily when automation could unlock substantial economic value, but does not identify uncertainty about the feasibility of full automation as a reason to invest early.

r005.rationale: It does not discuss using the observed slope of the automation curve to update beliefs about whether AI will achieve full automation.

fable-5.1.text:
So the main thing I'd say is that Tom's model was really built to answer one question, which is: how fast does the takeoff go once you start getting serious automation of AI R&D? And for that purpose it works reasonably well. But it treats a lot of things as exogenous that we thought actually matter a lot for the overall picture.

The biggest one is investment. In Tom's model you basically have a schedule for how much compute gets spent, how much goes into R&D, and that's an input you set by hand. Whereas in reality, the amount of money that flows into AI depends on what people expect the returns to be. If you think automating a large chunk of the economy is going to be worth tens of trillions of dollars, then you're willing to build enormous amounts of compute, train very expensive models, build data centers, and so on. And conversely if the returns look disappointing, investment slows down. So we wanted a model where investment, compute, R&D effort, and automation all get determined jointly, in a kind of general equilibrium sense, rather than having the economic side just be an afterthought.

The other thing is that Tom's model is quite focused on the AI R&D feedback loop, the idea that AI automates AI research and you get a software-driven acceleration. We think that's an important channel, but it's not obviously the dominant one. A lot of the acceleration could come from the more boring route, where AI just makes the economy more productive, that generates more output, more output means more investment in compute and hardware, and that compounds. And if you only model the software loop, you can end up with timelines and takeoff dynamics that look quite different from what you'd get if you take the broader economic feedback seriously.

So GATE, which stands for growth and AI transition endogenous, is trying to be something more like a standard growth model that an economist would recognize, with a production function, capital accumulation, a representative agent making investment decisions under some expectation of the future, and then with AI capabilities plugged in as something that gets produced by spending on compute and research. And the hope is that this lets you ask questions that the earlier model couldn't really ask, like: how does the behavior of the agents change if they believe automation is coming? How sensitive is the whole thing to the elasticity of substitution between tasks? What happens if hardware progress stalls out?

I'd also say we wanted something that was more transparent about its assumptions. When you run these models, the results are very sensitive to a handful of parameters, and I think it's valuable to have a framework where you can see which parameters are doing the work. So a big part of the motivation was less "Tom got it wrong" and more "let's build the version where the economics is actually in the model, and see what changes."

r001.rationale: The response says compute and R&D spending are endogenous in GATE, but does not explain how Davidson’s model maps effective compute increases to the share of tasks automated.

r002.rationale: It motivates making investment and other economic quantities endogenous and mentions a representative agent, but does not identify utility or value optimization as the central replacement for hardcoded decision rules.

r003.rationale: The response does not say Davidson’s hardcoded rules could yield unreasonable decisions under extreme parameter values.

r004.rationale: The response does not connect early AI investment to resolving uncertainty about whether full automation is feasible.

r005.rationale: The response does not describe the automation curve’s observed slope as evidence for updating beliefs about whether AI can achieve full automation.

astra-6.text:
The main motivation was to make the economics of automation more explicit. In a model like Tom Davidson’s, you make assumptions about how much compute it takes to train an AI that can automate a given fraction of tasks. That’s useful, but being able to automate a task doesn’t necessarily mean that doing so is economical. You also need to ask how much it costs to run the AI, how productive it is, and how that compares with employing a human.

Those decisions also depend on what’s happening in the rest of the economy. If many firms start using AI, demand for compute goes up. If some kinds of labor become more valuable because they complement AI, wages can rise. So the profitability of automation isn’t something you can determine once and then hold fixed.

With GATE, we wanted those choices and feedback effects to be part of the model. The point wasn’t simply to get a faster or slower takeoff than Tom’s model, but to understand how technical capabilities translate into actual deployment and economic growth.

r001.rationale: The response says Davidson’s model assumes how much compute is needed to automate a given fraction of tasks, but does not explain that increases in effective compute map to increases in the automated share.

r002.rationale: It describes making automation economics explicit, but does not identify replacing hardcoded decision rules with utility or value optimization.

r003.rationale: It does not mention hardcoded rules producing unreasonable decisions under extreme parameter values.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss uncertainty about full automation or early investment motivated by that uncertainty.

r005.rationale: It does not describe the automation curve’s observed slope as evidence for updating beliefs about full automation.

sol-6.1.text:
The motivation was to understand how much the results depend on the economic assumptions. In Tom’s model, there are some fairly simplified rules governing how firms invest in AI and how they deploy it. Those are useful for making the model tractable, but if you’re studying a transition as dramatic as widespread automation, those choices can matter a lot.

For example, being able to automate a task doesn’t necessarily mean it’s economical to automate it immediately. You have to ask how much compute it takes, what that compute costs, and how that compares with paying a human to do the task. And the compute you use to run AI systems has an opportunity cost: you could potentially use it for training or research instead.

So with GATE, we wanted to make those tradeoffs more explicit and let automation emerge from the economic decisions in the model. The point wasn’t that Tom’s model was useless—it was a very useful starting point—but to see which conclusions about AI-driven growth survive when you change the way those decisions are represented.

r001.rationale: The response discusses economic decisions about automation but does not explain a mapping from increases in effective compute to increases in the share of tasks automated.

r002.rationale: It says GATE makes tradeoffs explicit and lets automation emerge from economic decisions, but does not identify utility or value optimization replacing hardcoded rules as a central motivation.

r003.rationale: The response does not say that Davidson’s rules could produce unreasonable decisions under extreme parameter values.

r004.rationale: It does not identify uncertainty about full automation as a possible reason to invest in AI early.

r005.rationale: It does not discuss the automation curve’s slope as evidence people could use to update beliefs about full automation.
